title: The hem of his garment (Mark 5:21–34)
hook: a woman bleeding twelve years touches his cloak in the crowd; he stops to find her

segments.voice: Yesterday, a healed man begged to follow and was sent home to tell it across the Decapolis instead. Your line was tell the people who knew you.

Back across the lake, a crowd is waiting. A synagogue leader named Jairus pushes through, falls at Jesus's feet and begs: my little daughter is dying. Come. And Jesus goes, with the whole crowd pressing around him, shoulder to shoulder, jostling down a narrow street. A child's life is on the line. And somewhere in that crush is a woman nobody is looking at. She's been bleeding for twelve years. She's spent everything on doctors and only gotten worse. She doesn't want a scene. She just wants to reach one hand through.
screen: `JAIRUS: MY DAUGHTER IS DYING.` → `A CRUSH OF PEOPLE.` → `ONE HAND REACHES THROUGH.`

segments.voice: Mark slows down for her. In the King James Bible she "had suffered many things of many physicians, and had spent all that she had, and was nothing bettered, but rather grew worse." That sentence could have been written today, about a long illness or a stack of medical bills. Under the purity laws of the time, a condition like hers also made ordinary life complicated: worship, touch, closeness. So she makes a quiet plan. "If I may touch but his clothes, I shall be whole." She touches his cloak from behind, and immediately the bleeding stops. She can feel it. Then the turn: Jesus stops. In the middle of an emergency, with a dying child waiting, he asks, "Who touched my clothes?" His disciples point out the obvious: look at this crowd, and you ask who touched you? But he keeps looking. And she comes forward, shaking, falls down, and tells him the whole truth. His first word to her: "Daughter." "Daughter, thy faith hath made thee whole; go in peace, and be whole of thy plague." He could have let her slip away healed. Instead he made sure she was seen, named family, and sent off in peace in front of everyone. Notice the numbers: she's been ill twelve years. Jairus's daughter, we'll learn tomorrow, is twelve years old. Mark wraps one story inside the other. One small thing: the hem in today's title comes from Matthew and Luke. Mark just says his clothes.
screen: `MANY PHYSICIANS, NOTHING BETTERED.` · `IF I MAY TOUCH BUT HIS CLOTHES.` · `WHO TOUCHED MY CLOTHES?` · `DAUGHTER, GO IN PEACE.`

segments.voice: Picture a crowd you move through every day, a hallway, a store, a street, a group chat, and look for the person nobody's looking at: the one who's been tired for years, the one who reaches out quietly and then pulls back. Let one face come, and imagine stopping, turning around, asking a real question and waiting for the whole truth. If you pray, you can pray for that person now.
Cloak, what a woman ill for twelve years reached for in the crowd, and the reason Jesus stopped to find her and call her daughter.
Your line: daughter, go in peace. He stopped a whole crowd for one woman. That's day one hundred seventy-eight.

howItsDone: Many Christians pray for the chronically ill with this story in mind, and some churches offer prayer for healing with the laying on of hands or anointing with oil, alongside medical care.

notes: Editor review 2026-10-01: cut the superlatives ('more detail than almost anyone's', 'the only person he calls daughter', 'favorite storytelling moves'), the invented 'almost laugh', 'on purpose', and the line telling listeners they know the sentence.
Purity laws (Leviticus 15:25–27) phrased carefully ('made ordinary life complicated'); scholars caution against overstating her exclusion or framing Judaism negatively. Confirm tone.
'In Mark, she's the only person he calls daughter': confirm (Mark 5:34 is the only direct address as 'daughter' in Mark).
Mark 5:27 'touched his garment' (himation); 'hem/border' (kraspedon) is in Matthew 9:20 and Luke 8:44. Confirm.
